storm.summary_layperson: There are some radar echoes to the north over Fairfield County, but they're all moving away from Riverside, not toward it — tonight's 5–10 PM window should stay dry with only a low chance of a stray shower.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound is actually a bit warmer than the air right now (about 3°F), so there's no marine-layer buffer at all this evening — it doesn't matter tonight since nothing is tracking toward the cove anyway.
storm.detail_html:
Radar out of KOKX shows a cluster of cells to the north and NNE of Riverside, including a couple of stronger cores (up to 50 dBZ) around 22–25 miles out and a smaller pair just 5–8 miles away at 42–46 dBZ. None of them are a threat: every tracked cell has a negative closing speed, meaning the whole cluster is pulling away to the north rather than approaching the cove. The arrival-prediction engine finds no cell actually closing on Greenwich Cove right now.

Instability is weak — CAPE is only 250–380 J/kg across the next few forecast hours, well under the threshold where storms can intensify on their own, even though deep-layer shear is strong (55 kt). Strong shear with weak CAPE mostly organizes what's already there rather than spawning new development, which fits what radar is showing: an existing, departing cluster rather than a build-up.

The Sound's usual protective marine layer isn't a factor either way tonight. The air–water gap (the Sound holds heat, so cooler evening air over 74°F water) is already negative — the water is about 3°F warmer than the air — so there's no meaningful buffer for the pipeline to lean on. That's a moot point this evening since nothing is inbound to blunt.

Most likely outcome for the 5–10 PM window: dry, with the existing rain staying well north and east of Riverside. There's a slight chance (per the NWS short-range forecast) of an isolated shower, consistent with the general area of showers nearby, but nothing organized is aimed at the cove. What would change this call: any new cell development closer to the coast, or the departing cluster's outflow triggering fresh convection that tracks back south — radar would flag either quickly.

wind.regime_label: Light gradient wind — no sea breeze, direction may wander
wind.tactics_blurb: Light ENE-to-NE gradient wind with no sea breeze in play — the breeze backs toward N through the evening and fades below 3 kt by 8 PM. Favor the center of the course; there's no strong shore-shelter play in this direction, and by the back half of the window expect fully variable, drifter-class conditions.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a gradient-only day, not a sea-breeze day. The two-ingredient sea-breeze test needs both a land–water temperature gap of at least 5°F and a building thermal signal — the air–water differential is actually negative (about −3°F, water warmer than air) and only 20% of coastal stations show any southerly component, so neither ingredient is close to being met. That puts this window in Regime B-light: light synoptic wind with no thermal contribution, magnitude around 6–7 kt at the open-water gauges (`mean_speed_authoritative_kt` = 6.8 kt) and already easing fast in the HRRR sequence.

Direction starts ENE/NE, which by cove geography is on the cleaner, more offshore-laminar side of the compass — normally good for steady "cold breeze" racing. But at this magnitude, already backing and dropping through the HRRR sequence (7.5 → 6.5 → 4.4 → 2.3 kt from 4 PM to 7 PM, direction backing from ENE through NE to NNE), there isn't enough pressure left for that character to matter. Favor the center of the course over committing hard to either shore.

Worth flagging: current station obs (western-LIS cluster, RYC included) are reading E around 100°, while HRRR's own forecast direction for this hour is ENE at 58° — a 42° gap. On a sea-breeze day this would trigger the maturation correction, but that correction only applies in Regime A/A+; tonight it doesn't apply since there's no thermal engine running. Trust the current obs (E, ~100°) for right now, and lean on HRRR's own backing trend for how the next few hours should evolve, since that's the only forward-looking signal available.

The HRRR forecast only extends cleanly through about 7 PM tonight (forecast hours beyond that came back unavailable this run); the 8–10 PM rows are extrapolated from the observed backing/decay trend rather than model-forecast, so treat them as lower confidence. Because there's no thermal engine to collapse at sunset, the wind won't drop suddenly — it's simply continuing the fade it's already in, likely into fully variable, sub-2-kt conditions by the second half of the window. Fleet impact: 4–7 kt at the start is manageable club-racing breeze; by 9–10 PM this is drifter/light-air specialist territory with real postponement risk.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast hours beyond ~7:00 PM EDT (f05–f12) were unavailable this run — the 8:00–10:00 PM wind rows are trend-extrapolated, not model-forecast, and carry lower confidence.
Station direction agreement across the full ensemble is moderate-to-low (0.50) — the regional wind field is somewhat fragmented rather than one coherent flow.
